after: > [!check] Objectives
> 1.  Describe cranial nerve anatomy and function.
> 2.  Predict symptoms of cranial nerve pathology.
The [[cranial nerves]] are paired bundles of nerve fibres that exit the cranial cavity.

These nerves are either <mark class="hltr-blue">sensory afferents</mark>, <mark class="hltr-green">motor efferents</mark>, <mark class="hltr-pink">parasympathetic autonomic efferents</mark>, or a mixture. Note that the cranial nerves can only CARRY <mark class="hltr-orange">sympathetic signals</mark> → the sympathetic signals CANNOT originate here because the sympathetic autonomic efferents because those originate at the ***thoracolumbar regions*** instead of the craniosacral regions.
> [!orange] Sympathetic Innervation of the Head
> If sympathetic neurons don't originate until the thoracic spinal cord, how does the head and neck receive sympathetic innervation?
> -  pre-synaptic sympathetic neuron in the thoracolumbar region
> - travels up the [[sympathetic trunk]]
> - exits the spinal cord and synapses in the [[cervical ganglia]]
> - travels alongside other nerves (including [[cranial nerves]]) to reach its target

after: > [!check] Objectives
> **Identify the important functional anatomy of the upper extremity, as it pertains to clinical presentations of arm pathology.**
> - Identify the major muscles of the upper extremity (ie. shoulder girdle, brachium, forearm muscles originating from the medial and lateral epicondyles, hand muscles)
The **arm** extends from the shoulder to the elbow. There are fascial layers within the arm that divide it into compartments, which have distinct functions and innervation patterns.
- deep to the skin and subcutaneous tissue is the deep fascia of the arm, the **brachial fascia**

- two **intermuscular septa** (medial and lateral) run from the brachial fascia to the humerus and divide the arm into an anterior and a posterior compartment, each its own functional and innervation unit
> [!multi-column]
>> [!blank]
> >> [!light-blue] Anterior Compartment of the Arm
> >> - **functions**: shoulder flexion, elbow flexion, supination
> >> - **innervation**: [[musculocutaneous nerve]]
> >> - **contents**: [[biceps brachii muscle]], [[coracobrachialis muscle]], [[brachialis muscle]]
> >>[!blank]
> >> [!pink] Posterior Compartment of the Arm
> >> - **functions**: shoulder extension, elbow extension
> >> - **innervation**: [[radial nerve]]
> >> - **contents**: [[triceps brachii muscle]]

The **forearm** extends from the cubital fossa to the wrist. are split into distinct compartments. Just like in the arm, fascial layers of the forearm divide it into compartments, with distinct functions and innervation patterns.

- NOTE - these compartments are named "<font color="#00b0f0">anterior</font>" and "<font color="#e424b7">posterior</font>" ***because of where their muscles are attaching*** - despite being situated medially and laterally.
> [!multi-column]
> >[!pink] Posterior Compartment of the Forearm
> >- **functions**: extension of the wrist and hand, supination of the forearm
> >- **innervation**: [[radial nerve]]
> >- **contents**: 11 extensor-supinators in 2 layers (superficial 6, deep 5), plus anconeus
> > [!light-blue] Anterior Compartment of the Forearm
> >- **functions**: flexion of the wrist and hand, pronation of the forearm

> >- **innervation**: [[median nerve]] (except for 1½ muscles: the [[flexor carpi ulnaris muscle]] and the medial half of the [[flexor digitorum profundus muscle]], to digits 4 and 5, which are innervated by the [[ulnar nerve]])
> >- **contents**: 8 flexor-pronators in 3 layers (superficial 4, intermediate 1, deep 3)
